column5: Lights mark days, years, and appointed seasons
column6: The commentary joins night and day to longer seasonal and lifetime intervals; Genesis assigns the lights the work of marking days, years, and appointed times, making several scales of time depend on the same cycle.

column5: Sun returns after setting
column6: The commentary treats morning and late day as recurring joined pieces; Ecclesiastes has the sun rise, set, and hurry back to the place of its rising.

column5: Moon marks appointed times and sun its setting
column6: The commentary places seasonal middles alongside daily transitions; the psalm says the moon was made for appointed times while the sun knows its setting.

column5: Human years swept away like sleep
column6: The commentary names a short sleep and says a long human span is later perceived as brief; the psalm says God sweeps humans away like sleep before its morning-grass comparison.

column5: Morning growth withers by evening
column6: The commentary compresses a life into the morning-to-evening interval; the psalm's grass flourishes in the morning and fades by evening, completing the time image begun in the preceding verse.

column5: Long night spent waiting for dawn
column6: The commentary develops broken sleep, morning and evening, and patience stretched between them; Job describes lying down, waiting to rise, and tossing through a seemingly prolonged night until dawn.

column5: Waiting more than watchmen for morning
column6: The commentary turns patience into a posture held across night toward morning; the psalmist repeats that his soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for morning.

column5: Accumulated wealth cannot go through death
column6: The commentary recalls multiplying possessions until the grave; the psalm says a wealthy person carries none of it away when dying, specifying the limit that accumulation cannot cross.

column5: Riches fail at reckoning, righteousness delivers
column6: The commentary puts accumulated goods beside righteous deeds and final loss; the proverb says wealth is useless on the day of wrath while righteousness delivers from death.

column5: Dust returns but spirit returns to God
column6: The commentary reports the denial that passing time alone destroys humans and recalls final accountability; Ecclesiastes instead says the body returns to dust and the spirit returns to the God who gave it.

column5: The long dead awaken for judgment
column6: The commentary's brief-seeming stay ends at a gathering where deniers lose; Daniel says many who sleep in the dust awaken, some to everlasting life and some to shame, supplying a direct alternative to death as time's final word.

column5: Youth faces later judgment
column6: The commentary names youth as one stage and ends with reckoning of a whole life; Ecclesiastes tells the young person to rejoice while young but to know God will bring these acts into judgment.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: decreeing justice
column6: The package's root table offers an unverified sound correspondence; Wisdom says rulers decree justice by her, linking the commentary's counsel in haqq to enacted right order rather than merely to a seasonal due date.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: annual perpetual ordinance
column6: The table offers an unverified sound correspondence; the exodus day is to be remembered as a festival through generations by perpetual חקה, making a fixed calendar date bind successive people.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: day-night covenant at its time
column6: The table's proposed sound correspondence is unverified; Jeremiah says the covenant with day and night would have to be broken for either to fail to come at its appointed time, tying the commentary's sequence to reliable recurrence.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: unjust decrees
column6: The table offers only a sound correspondence; Isaiah denounces those who inscribe unjust decrees, showing that a prescribed order can oppose the commentary's haqq and righteous action when its content is corrupt.

column5: Gathered festivals rejected without justice
column6: The commentary says a community persists through righteous conduct, truth, and patience; Amos has God reject its festivals and solemn assemblies, complicating the assumption that recurring gatherings alone preserve a people.

column5: Justice must flow continually
column6: The commentary joins truthful counsel to the group's endurance; after rejecting festivals Amos calls for justice to roll like water and righteousness like an enduring stream, identifying the needed practice beyond assembly.

column5: One hour of repentance and good deeds
column6: The commentary says long earthly time contracts to an hour and makes righteous action decisive; Avot values one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world while separately valuing an hour of the coming world's peace.

column5: If the dead do not rise, eat and drink
column6: The commentary reports deniers who treat mortal time as final; Paul voices the practical conclusion of denying resurrection, eating and drinking because tomorrow brings death, then challenges that premise in his resurrection argument.

column5: The dead rise according to deeds
column6: The commentary's final compressed stay ends in loss for deniers and survival through right action; Jesus says those in the tombs come out to resurrection of life or judgment according to what they have done.

column5: The dead judged from records of deeds
column6: The commentary reports that time itself is said to destroy and recalls an accounting after a brief-seeming stay; Revelation has the dead stand before the throne as books are opened and each is judged by deeds.

column5: Merchants plan a profitable year
column6: The commentary recalls competitive accumulation that hides life's shortness; James addresses people planning a year of travel and trade for gain, the precise plan exposed as uncertain in the next verse.

column5: Self-stored goods versus wealth toward God
column6: The commentary opposes multiplication of possessions to deeds that endure; Jesus closes the rich fool's story by contrasting storing up for oneself with being rich toward God.

column5: Delay produces sleep in a waiting group
column6: The commentary gives broken sleep a place between periods of waiting; in Jesus' bridegroom story the delay makes all the attendants drowsy and asleep before the decisive arrival.

column5: Prepared attendants enter before the door closes
column6: The commentary asks who remains when an apparently long wait abruptly ends; in the bridegroom story those prepared enter the feast on his arrival and the door is shut.

column5: Times and seasons introduce the final Day
column6: The commentary moves from named periods to a sudden terminal hour; Paul explicitly invokes times and seasons before describing the Lord's Day as unexpectedly arriving in the following verse.

column5: Steadfastness joined to enduring work
column6: The commentary's remaining group combines persistence with righteous deeds; Paul concludes his resurrection argument by telling believers to be steadfast and always active in the Lord's work because that labor is not futile.

column5: Human flesh as grass
column6: The commentary reduces a human lifetime to a passing interval; Peter applies Isaiah's fading-grass image to all flesh, making mortal brevity part of his appeal to a community born through the gospel.

column5: Enduring word against passing life
column6: The commentary joins short human life to truth that can hold people together; Peter completes the Isaiah citation by contrasting fading humanity with the Lord's enduring word and identifies that word with what was proclaimed to his hearers.

column5: A new Today after a long time
column6: The commentary describes time as linked parts in which an appeal remains open; Hebrews says God appoints another day called Today after a long time, using David's warning to demand a present response.

column5: Now is the accepted time and day of rescue
column6: The commentary's finite interval calls for righteous response before the end; Paul applies a promise about the favorable time and salvation day to his hearers' present now.

column5: Keep watch because the hour is unknown
column6: The commentary stretches patience through uncertain time before the final contraction; the Didache tells believers to watch their lives and keep lamps ready since they do not know the Lord's hour.

column5: Meet often; faith must endure to the end
column6: The commentary connects repeated meetings among people with the need to remain through time; the Didache urges frequent gathering for the soul and says a lifetime of faith is of no benefit unless completed at the end.

column5: Lights govern day and night and distinguish them
column6: The commentary holds night and day together without dissolving their distinction; Genesis says the lights govern the two periods and separate light from darkness, adding ordered difference to their succession.

column5: Sun governs the day
column6: The commentary's two daily periods are each assigned a place; the litany names the sun as ruler of the day, with its companion night assignment in the next verse.

column5: Moon and stars govern the night
column6: The commentary pairs night with day as adjacent ordered parts; the litany gives the night to moon and stars after naming the sun's daily rule in the preceding verse.

column5: Horn blown at recurring lunar feast
column6: The commentary extends morning-evening segments to prescribed seasonal observance; the psalm orders the horn at new moon and full moon for the festival day, whose status as statute is given in the next verse.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: festival statute
column6: The root table supplies an unverified sound correspondence; the festival marked in the preceding verse is called a חק for Israel, connecting a recurring appointed day to a shared obligation.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: enduring cosmic decree
column6: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; God establishes the heavenly bodies permanently and gives them a decree that will not pass, an ordinance behind the commentary's dependable recurring periods.

column5: Mortal grass fades while divine word stands
column6: The commentary joins a vanishing human lifespan to the truth that sustains the community; Isaiah says the grass withers and flower fades but God's word remains forever.

column5: Acceptable fasting frees the oppressed
column6: The commentary ties calendrical practice to righteous action; Isaiah defines God's chosen fast as releasing unjust bonds and freeing the oppressed, giving a concrete ethical test for a designated day.

column5: Humans do not know their fatal time
column6: The commentary says a long life can suddenly end in a fraction of a day; Ecclesiastes says people do not know their time and compares their capture by disaster to fish and birds trapped unexpectedly.

column5: Nighttime recitation has a bounded interval
column6: The commentary makes night a distinct period filled with a sustained religious act; the Mishnah asks when the evening Shema is read and sets competing limits within the night's watches.

column5: Morning recitation begins with visible dawn
column6: The commentary joins morning to the night before it as a new part of disciplined time; the Mishnah asks when morning Shema begins and uses the ability to distinguish colors to mark the transition.

column5: Fixed instruction must become deeds
column6: The commentary couples counsel in truth with righteous works; Shammai says to make Torah study regular, speak little, and do much, specifying how words and acts should be ordered across ordinary time.

column5: Continue the work though it cannot be finished
column6: The commentary's patient group persists across a life too short to encompass everything; Avot says one need not finish the work but is not free to abandon it.

column5: Prepare in this life's antechamber
column6: The commentary treats mortal time as a bounded span before the final meeting; Avot likens this world to an antechamber where one prepares before entering the coming world's hall.

column5: Righteous souls ask how long they must wait
column6: The commentary links patient waiting to the final reckoning; the souls of the righteous ask from their chambers when the reward will arrive, making the interval after death itself a question. Numbering of 4 Ezra varies by edition.

column5: Waiting ends when the number is complete
column6: The commentary says people remain linked through a long interval before its end; the angel's reply makes the completion of the number of the righteous the limit of their wait. Numbering of 4 Ezra varies by edition.

column5: The present form of the world is passing
column6: The commentary says a seemingly stable span is already vanishing; Paul tells those engaged with the world not to live as though its present form were lasting.

column5: Servants wait to admit the returning master
column6: The commentary links people through patient readiness during uncertain time; Jesus compares disciples to servants waiting for their master so they can open immediately when he arrives.

column5: Unknown day and hour demand watchfulness
column6: The commentary compresses the end of a long interval into an unexpected moment; the bridegroom parable concludes with an instruction to stay awake because the day and hour are unknown.

column5: Night-and-day prayer seeks to strengthen others
column6: The commentary makes mutual support stretch through both parts of the day; Paul describes earnest night-and-day prayer to see his hearers again and supply what their faith lacks.

column5: Night-and-day labor spares the community
column6: The commentary connects righteous work across the daily cycle with people sustaining one another; Paul says his group worked night and day so they would burden none of the believers.

column5: An aged witness awaits a promise before death
column6: The commentary sets divine promise within the finite span of a life; Simeon has been told he will not see death before seeing the Messiah, making his later waiting answer a personal life limit.

column5: One hour compared with the whole day's labor
column6: The commentary compresses a long stay to an hour and asks what deeds count at its end; the first workers complain that those hired last worked only one hour yet received an equal wage, a parabolic comparison rather than a statement that all lives are equally long.

column5: Past, present, and future held in the mind
column6: The commentary argues that lived time consists of joined pieces rather than a single flat flow; Augustine describes a present of remembered past, attended present, and expected future, offering a later Christian account of how those parts are connected.

column5: Good not withheld from upright walkers
column6: The commentary makes righteous conduct the condition of continuing good through time; the psalm says God withholds no good from those who walk uprightly. The verb uses Hebrew עצר, the package's sound correspondence to Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r, but restraint here has no established cognate link to the commentary's time sense.

column5: The impious call life short and death final
column6: The commentary reports those who think time alone destroys them; Wisdom assigns to its impious speakers the claim that life is short and no remedy follows death, but the book frames their reasoning as unsound.
